title: Ulyana and the Hymn
premise: Gideon Underhill hosts the overnight shift at a small-town AM station where callers sometimes turn out to be people who died within the week, and his careful rituals—counted doors, kept lights—keep him safely invisible to whatever uses the frequency. When his childhood imaginary friend Ulyana appears on his porch, unchanged after thirty years, he learns she was never imaginary: she is a fragment of the hymn the town's founders sang to bind something beneath the water tower, and the binding is failing. The founders' descendants have been feeding it grief through the radio for decades, and Gideon's dead callers are its harvest. To save the town he must finish the interrupted ritual himself—an act that will make him visible to everything he has spent his life hiding from—and in the final broadcast he sings the last verse with Ulyana, trading his anonymity and nearly his life to seal the thing away, though the cost is that no one will ever remember he existed except her.
about_author: Felix Lockridge is the pen name of a former late-night radio engineer who spent six years working the board at a 1,000-watt AM station in upstate New York before turning to fiction. He writes horror about small towns, old frequencies, and the things that wait politely just outside the porch light.

chapters.title: The Dead Air Shift
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. On the overnight show, Gideon takes a call from Mrs. Halloran, who mentions her own funeral; he checks his ritual—lights on, doors counted—and stays calm on air. The chapter establishes his rules of invisibility and ends with dread: the dead are calling more often than they used to.

chapters.title: Counting Doors
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. We learn his childhood: a mother who vanished, an imaginary friend named Ulyana, and the first time he learned that being unnoticed keeps you safe. A second dead caller describes the water tower singing. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as discipline.

chapters.title: Someone on the Porch
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. At dawn, Ulyana is standing on his porch exactly as she looked at age eight, patient and wrong. She says only, 'You stopped singing.' He slams the door and counts it twice. Beat: terror braided with a shameful flicker of joy at being seen.

chapters.title: The Founders' Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Gideon, with a letter from 1931 in second-person flashback. In the station's archive he finds the founders' hymnal, its final verse torn out, and a photograph of nine townspeople—including someone with his mother's face. Beat: the past is closer than he thought.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: POV alternating between Gideon and a dead caller, Dale Pruitt. Dale describes the space between broadcasts—a warm dark place with a hymn playing underneath—and begs Gideon not to finish 'the song.' Beat: sympathy curdling into manipulation; the dead may not want saving.

chapters.title: Ulyana Explains Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Ulyana appears inside the locked studio, sitting in the guest chair, and answers every question with fragments of melody. She warns him the tower is 'thirsty' but refuses to say what for. Beat: the uncanny comfort of a friend who is also a trap.

chapters.title: The Descendants
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. He tracks the founding families to a single living member, Maribel Voss, who runs the funeral home. She recognizes the hymnbook instantly and goes pale: 'You're not supposed to know this exists.' Beat: the conspiracy has a human face and a tired one.

chapters.title: What the Tower Holds
chapters.summary: POV Maribel. Her family has fed the thing beneath the water tower for four generations—grief, funerals, names read aloud over the airwaves. The ritual broke in 1974 when the last singer died mid-verse. Beat: complicity; justice outside the law begins to look like inherited sin.

chapters.title: Static Sermon
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. During a storm, the station broadcasts by itself: the hymn, incomplete, looping. Every phone line lights up with dead voices singing harmony. Gideon holds the board steady because someone has to. Beat: duty as defiance; he chooses to stay at his post.

chapters.title: The Verse That Was Torn
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Maribel reveals the torn page went to the singer who died in 1974—Gideon's mother. The realization lands: he isn't an outsider; he's the missing heir. Beat: belonging arrives as a wound.

chapters.title: Invisible No More
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. The moment he touches the hymnbook, the town sees him—strangers greet him by name, dogs follow him, and something under the ground turns its attention like a searchlight. His lifelong armor becomes a target. Beat: power's terrible price of visibility.

chapters.title: Dale Comes Home
chapters.summary: POV Dale (dead) and Gideon. Dale's reanimated body appears at the station door, polite and dripping, asking to sing along. Gideon refuses, and the town's lights brown out in response. Beat: refusal as the first act of resistance.

chapters.title: Maribel's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Maribel. She admits the descendants could have ended it decades ago but chose the bargain: the thing protects the town from everything else. Power corrupts gently, one comfortable year at a time. Beat: moral rot revealed as ordinary convenience.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Ulyana teaches him the hymn in the empty studio at night, her voice layering over his like a second self. Each verse he learns, he remembers more of his childhood—and more of what his mother actually did. Beat: intimacy with the inhuman.

chapters.title: The Town That Watches
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Neighbors gather silently outside the station each night, smiling, waiting for the broadcast. Maribel warns him they aren't possessed—they're hopeful, which is worse. Beat: the horror of collective consent.

chapters.title: Interrupted Broadcast
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. Mid-show, the thing speaks through every caller at once, offering Gideon his mother back if he sings only the verses it likes. He nearly accepts. Ulyana cuts the transmitter herself. Beat: temptation, and the cost of being saved from your own wish.

chapters.title: Nineteen Seventy-Four
chapters.summary: POV Gideon, dream-vision. He relives the night his mother died mid-verse at the tower, sees the founders' ritual fail, and understands the final verse requires two singers—one living, one neither. Ulyana was made for this. Beat: grief transmuted into purpose.

chapters.title: The Last Door
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. He counts his doors one final time and leaves them all unlocked—the ritual of hiding is over. Maribel gives him the master key to the tower and stays behind to hold the phone lines open. Beat: quiet resolve before catastrophe.

chapters.title: Broadcast From the Tower
chapters.summary: POV Gideon. He hijacks the transmitter and sings from atop the water tower as the whole town listens, dead and living alike. The thing rises through the tank, wearing the faces of his callers, singing counterpoint. Beat: climax begins—courage against a chorus of the harvested.

chapters.title: The Final Verse
chapters.summary: POV Gideon and Ulyana together. The last verse demands a name freely given; Gideon offers his own, and Ulyana joins on the harmony she was created to hold. The thing is bound again—but the song starts taking his memories as payment. Beat: sacrifice in real time.

chapters.title: After the Sign-Off
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana. Dawn. The town wakes remembering nothing of the week; the station plays music; Maribel alone keeps a locked drawer of notes she can't explain. Gideon sits on the studio floor, half-erased, while Ulyana holds his hand. Beat: aftermath, tender and hollow.

chapters.title: Ulyana and the Hymn
chapters.summary: POV Ulyana. She cannot restore what the song took, but she can remember for both of them. Each night she tells Gideon who he is, story by story, and he slowly believes her. The final image: two figures on a lit porch, doors counted, singing softly so nothing hears. Beat: belonging found in the smallest possible audience.
